newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nippon Life sees no rapid reversal in weak yen.
newsitem.headline: Nippon Life sees no rapid reversal in weak yen.

text.p: Nippon Life Insurance Co, Japan's largest insurer, said on Tuesday that it does not expect a rapid reversal in the weak yen trend in the short-term.
Tomohiro Kawase, director of Nippon Life's Finance & Investment Planning Office, told Reuters in an interview that the company would increase its holdings of foreign-currency denominated securities.

"We are not betting on a scenario of a rapidly weakening yen (from the current level). But taking account of the gap between Japanese and U.S. interest rates, it is unlikely the yen will rapidly appreciate (in the short-term)," Kawase said.

He said Nippon Life, one of Japan's biggest institutional investors, had not worked out any target for an increase in its weighting in foreign bonds. However, he said the company would increase the weighting over the coming two to three years because it expected returns on foreign bond investments to be better than those from local stocks.
Kawase said that in the past few years, the proportion of Nippon Life's foreign bond holdings had fluctuated between four and five percent of its total investment portfolio.

Kawase said Nippon Life had been critical of equity financing conducted by Japanese banks in order to cope with the international capital adequacy ratio requirement set under the auspices of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).

"We are critical of banks' equity-financing," he said. Banks should take measures to cut risk-weighted assets to cope with the international capital adequacy ratio, rather than only taking steps to increase capital, he said.

After posting losses in the 1995/96 business year due to active write-offs of problem loans, several major Japanese banks issued preferred stock last year to help increase their capital adequacy ratios.
Many regional banks also decided to issue new shares to existing shareholders at a price between the market value and the face value to increase their capital ratios in 1996/97.

Kawase said Nippon Life did not buy any preferred stocks issued by Japanese banks at home or abroad last year, and when it bought new shares issued by a bank, it sold the same amount of shares in the bank.

Kawase said Nippon Life planned to maintain the value of its stockholdings at the current level but continue to pay attention to companies with better business prospects and to cut its weighting in the banking sector.
"Basically, the banking, transport and heavy industry sectors are overweighted in our equity portfolio," he said.
Maintaining the value of stockholdings meant the weighting of stocks in Nippon Life's investment portfolio would fall in line with rises in the firm's assets, he said.
